Reference: Donaldson and Hornbeck (2016)

Model Setting

The paper asks how much railroads mattered for the United States economy, and in particular for the agricultural sector in 1890. Fogel (1964) answered with a social saving calculation and concluded that the aggregate effect was small, because waterways and canals were only moderately more expensive on most routes. Later work compared counties that received railroads with counties that did not, which identifies relative effects only: when the network is extended to one county, every other county is affected through trade, so there is no untreated control group. The paper's solution is to measure the treatment by each county's market access, a reduced-form expression derived from a general equilibrium trade model in the tradition of Eaton and Kortum (2002), extended to include immobile land, mobile capital and mobile labor. In the model the equilibrium land rental rate of a county is log-linear in one endogenous county-specific variable, market access, which summarizes all direct and indirect effects of the national matrix of trade costs. Market access rises when it becomes cheaper to trade with another county, and more so when that county is populous.

The authors build a network database of railroads, canals, natural waterways and wagon routes, compute lowest-cost freight routes between all pairs of counties in 1870 and 1890, and regress changes in log agricultural land value on changes in log market access for 2,327 counties. A 1 percent increase in market access raises land value by about 0.51 percent. Removing all railroads in 1890 lowers market access by 80 percent on average and is estimated to lower the total value of agricultural land by 60.2 percent, an annual loss equal to 3.22 percent of GNP, moderately above Fogel's bound of 2.7 percent. Fogel's proposed canal extensions would have mitigated only 13 percent of this loss and improved country roads 21 percent. When the model is solved in full, removing railroads also implies large falls in total population (if worker utility is fixed) or in worker utility (if total population is fixed), losses that land values alone do not capture.

Fogel's Social Saving Benchmark

Fogel (1964) estimated that the social saving from railroads in agriculture in 1890 was no more than 2.7 percent of GNP: 0.6 percent from inter-regional trade (from 9 primary markets in the Midwest to 90 secondary markets in the East and South) and 2.1 percent from intraregional trade (from farms to primary markets). The inter-regional figure of 73 million dollars multiplies the difference in freight costs with and without railroads by the quantities shipped in 1890; it is an upper bound because it treats transport demand as perfectly inelastic. For intraregional trade, railroads mainly shortened expensive wagon hauls. Fogel called land more than 40 miles from a navigable waterway the infeasible region and bounded the loss there by its annual land rent, about 154 million dollars; adding 94 million dollars of higher transport costs in the feasible region gives 248 million dollars. The total of 321 million dollars compares with 642 million dollars, or 5.35 percent of GNP, for the loss of all agricultural land. Land values are converted to annual flows with Fogel's preferred mortgage interest rate of 7.91 percent, and GNP in 1890 is taken to be 12 billion dollars. Fogel also argued that a feasible extension of the canal network would have mitigated 30 percent of the intraregional loss.

With digitized maps and county data the authors recompute the annual rent of the infeasible region as 186 million dollars, and find a return of only 5 million dollars on land more than 40 miles from a waterway or a railroad in 1890. Letting land value decay linearly between 0 and 40 miles from the nearest waterway or railroad gives an intraregional loss of 325 million dollars (2.7 percent of GNP) without railroads and 225 million dollars (1.9 percent) when railroads are replaced by the proposed canals, a mitigation of 31 percent. These exercises assume the relationship between land value and the transport network and assume where goods are shipped. The market access approach estimates the first and lets a trade model determine the second, while keeping Fogel's insight that the price of the immobile factor capitalizes the cost of reaching markets.

Preferences, Technology and Trade Costs

The economy consists of many trading counties, indexed by ooo when the origin of a trade and by ddd when the destination. There is one sector (an extension with agriculture, manufacturing and input-output linkages is in the Online Appendix). Agents consume a continuum of differentiated varieties indexed by jjj, with CES tastes and elasticity of substitution σ\sigmaσ. A consumer in county ooo with income YoY_oYo​ facing the price vector Po\mathbf{P}_oPo​ has indirect utility:

Po≡[∫0n(po(j))1−σdj]11−σ(2)P_o\equiv\left[\int_0^n\left(p_o(j)\right)^{1-\sigma}dj\right]^{\frac{1}{1-\sigma}} \tag{2}Po​≡[∫0n​(po​(j))1−σdj]1−σ1​(2)

Producers use a Cobb-Douglas technology in land, labor and capital under perfect competition. The marginal cost of producing variety jjj in county ooo is:

MCo(j)=qoαwoγro1−α−γzo(j)(3)MC_o(j)=\frac{q_o^{\alpha}w_o^{\gamma}r_o^{1-\alpha-\gamma}}{z_o(j)} \tag{3}MCo​(j)=zo​(j)qoα​woγ​ro1−α−γ​​(3)

The paper prints the distribution function as 1−exp⁡(−Aoz−θ)1-\exp(-A_oz^{-\theta})1−exp(−Ao​z−θ), which is decreasing in zzz and is the probability that a draw exceeds zzz; the form above is the Eaton-Kortum distribution function on which the price index and gravity results below rest. Trade is subject to iceberg trade costs: a variety made in ooo that sells locally for poo(j)p_{oo}(j)poo​(j) sells in ddd for pod(j)=τodpoo(j)p_{od}(j)=\tau_{od}p_{oo}(j)pod​(j)=τod​poo​(j), with τod≥1\tau_{od}\geq1τod​≥1. Remote counties pay high prices for imported varieties and receive low prices for the varieties they produce.

Factor Mobility

Three assumptions on factor markets close the model. Land is immobile and in fixed supply LoL_oLo​, set by county borders. Landowners need not live where they own land; land rents are assumed to be spent in proportion to county populations. Capital is perfectly mobile, so ro=rr_o=rro​=r in every county, and the United States faces a perfectly elastic supply of capital (for the general equilibrium counterfactuals the nominal price of capital is fixed relative to the price index of New York City). Labor is perfectly mobile across counties, at least over many years, so utility is equalized and nominal wages satisfy:

wo=UˉPo(5)w_o=\bar{U}P_o \tag{5}wo​=UˉPo​(5)

where Uˉ\bar{U}Uˉ is the common level of worker utility. The level of Uˉ\bar{U}Uˉ does not affect the regressions, because changes in it are common to all counties in logs and are absorbed by the constant, but how Uˉ\bar{U}Uˉ is determined matters for the counterfactuals.

Prices and Trade Flows

Under perfect competition the price of a variety equals its marginal cost, and consumers buy each variety from the cheapest source. Eaton and Kortum (2002) then deliver two results. First, the price index of destination ddd satisfies:

(Pd)−θ=κ1∑oAo(qoαwoγ)−θτod−θ≡CMAd(6)\left(P_d\right)^{-\theta}=\kappa_1\sum_oA_o\left(q_o^{\alpha}w_o^{\gamma}\right)^{-\theta}\tau_{od}^{-\theta}\equiv CMA_d \tag{6}(Pd​)−θ=κ1​o∑​Ao​(qoα​woγ​)−θτod−θ​≡CMAd​(6)

with the constant:

κ1≡[Γ(θ+1−σθ)]−θ1−σr−(1−α−γ)θ(7)\kappa_1\equiv\left[\Gamma\left(\frac{\theta+1-\sigma}{\theta}\right)\right]^{-\frac{\theta}{1-\sigma}}r^{-(1-\alpha-\gamma)\theta} \tag{7}κ1​≡[Γ(θθ+1−σ​)]−1−σθ​r−(1−α−γ)θ(7)

It measures access to cheap products: a sum of the productivity-adjusted production costs of all origins that could supply ddd, with weights that decline in the trade cost τod\tau_{od}τod​. Trade costs affect trade flows with elasticity −θ-\theta−θ, holding fixed exporter factor prices, importer income and the importer's price index; this is why θ\thetaθ is called the trade elasticity.

Implications for Empirical Work

The rent equation has three implications. First, all forces that make goods and factor markets interdependent across counties are summarized by market access (holding Uˉ\bar{U}Uˉ fixed). If county A receives a railroad, the counties that trade with A, those that traded with A's old or new partners, and so on, are all affected. Even with random assignment of railroads a regression of land rents on railroad access would be biased for the aggregate effect, because the control counties are treated; a regression on market access is not, because every county's market access adjusts. The aggregate effect of a counterfactual network follows from inserting the counterfactual τod\tau_{od}τod​ into MAoMA_oMAo​ and then into the rent equation. Second, a county's market access changes with railroad construction far beyond its borders, so identification need not rely on the county's own, possibly endogenous, railroads. Third, a counterfactual network may change Uˉ\bar{U}Uˉ. With a perfectly elastic supply of international migrants, Uˉ\bar{U}Uˉ is pinned down abroad and the aggregate population N≡∑oNoN\equiv\sum_oN_oN≡∑o​No​ adjusts; with a perfectly inelastic supply, NNN is fixed and Uˉ\bar{U}Uˉ adjusts, which shifts all land rents through κ4\kappa_4κ4​ (the paper's note refers to κ3\kappa_3κ3​ in the rent equation). Reality lies between these extremes.

Taking the rent equation to data requires several steps. The Census reports the value of agricultural land, not its rent; it suffices that:

Vo=qor(19)V_o=\frac{q_o}{r} \tag{19}Vo​=rqo​​(19)

where VoV_oVo​ is land value and rrr a fixed interest rate, and the results are unaffected if the interest rate varies by county, by state-year or with the controls. The outcome is the total value of agricultural land in the county, with land not in farms assigned zero agricultural value; reported values are deflated by state to the pure value of land net of buildings and improvements, following Fogel, which lowers total land value by 39 percent. Productivity AoA_oAo​ is unobserved: its fixed component is differenced out and its changes are assumed orthogonal to changes in market access conditional on location controls.

Market access itself is not directly observed, because wages and productivities are not. Given data on populations NdN_dNd​ and trade costs, the market access system above consists of as many equations as counties and has a unique solution up to a scalar multiple, by results cited from Allen and Arkolakis (2014); it can be solved numerically. This is the model-derived market access. A simpler and less model-dependent measure is the first-order approximation:

MAo≈∑dτod−θNd(20)MA_o\approx\sum_d\tau_{od}^{-\theta}N_d \tag{20}MAo​≈d∑​τod−θ​Nd​(20)

a population-weighted, trade-cost-discounted sum that drops the term MAd−(1+θ)/θMA_d^{-(1+\theta)/\theta}MAd−(1+θ)/θ​. In logs it is highly correlated with the model-derived term. To limit the endogeneity that arises because population is determined jointly with land rents, a county's own population is excluded, and the variable used throughout the empirical analysis is MAo≡∑d≠oτod−θNdMA_o\equiv\sum_{d\neq o}\tau_{od}^{-\theta}N_dMAo​≡∑d=o​τod−θ​Nd​. The measure recalls the market potential of Harris (1954), which is effectively:

∑d≠o(τod)−1Nd(21)\sum_{d\neq o}\left(\tau_{od}\right)^{-1}N_d \tag{21}d=o∑​(τod​)−1Nd​(21)

with distance as a proxy for trade costs. The paper differs in using trade costs, so that the railroad network matters although distances are fixed, and in the exponent −θ-\theta−θ.

The trade elasticity is estimated by nonlinear least squares. Writing the rent equation at time ttt:

ln⁡qot=f(θ)ot+εot,f(θ)ot≡(1+γ1+αθ)ln⁡MA(θ)ot,εot≡(11+αθ)ln⁡(AotLot)(22)\ln q_{ot}=f(\theta)_{ot}+\varepsilon_{ot},\qquad f(\theta)_{ot}\equiv\left(\frac{1+\gamma}{1+\alpha\theta}\right)\ln MA(\theta)_{ot},\qquad\varepsilon_{ot}\equiv\left(\frac{1}{1+\alpha\theta}\right)\ln\left(\frac{A_{ot}}{L_{ot}}\right) \tag{22}lnqot​=f(θ)ot​+εot​,f(θ)ot​≡(1+αθ1+γ​)lnMA(θ)ot​,εot​≡(1+αθ1​)ln(Lot​Aot​​)(22)

where MA(θ)otMA(\theta)_{ot}MA(θ)ot​ solves the market access system for given θ\thetaθ, trade costs τodt\tau_{odt}τodt​ and populations NotN_{ot}Not​. With the land and labor shares set to α=0.19\alpha=0.19α=0.19 and γ=0.60\gamma=0.60γ=0.60 (Caselli and Coleman 2001) and a grid search over 1,000 values, conditional on the fixed effects and controls of the main specification, the estimate is θ=8.22\theta=8.22θ=8.22, with a 95 percent confidence interval from 3.73 to 26.83 (block bootstrap by state, 400 replications). The value is close to the preferred estimate of 8.28 in Eaton and Kortum (2002), whose extreme estimates are 3.60 and 12.86.

Network Database and Trade Costs

County-to-county trade costs come from a GIS network database with three components: cost parameters per unit length for each mode, a network that records where freight could move, and the computation of lowest-cost routes. The cost parameters follow Fogel:

  • Railroads: 0.63 cents per ton-mile.

  • Waterways: 0.49 cents per ton-mile, which includes insurance for lost cargo (0.025 cents), storage and inventory costs of slower transport and winter closure (0.194 cents) and the social cost of public waterway investment (0.073 cents).

  • Transshipment: 50 cents per ton whenever goods are transferred to or from a railroad car, river boat, canal barge or ocean liner.

  • Wagons: 23.1 cents per ton-mile of straight-line distance, that is 16.5 cents per mile traveled times Fogel's adjustment factor of 1.4.

Ten miles by wagon cost roughly as much as 375 to 475 miles by railroad or waterway, so the measured costs are dominated by the required wagon distances, as Fogel (1964) and Fishlow (1965) stressed. The network is built in four steps. Digitized railroad maps for 1870 and 1890 (from Atack and coauthors) are corrected so that travel is possible through the network and turns are allowed at intersections. Canals, navigable rivers (Fogel's definition) and routes across lakes and oceans are added; they do not change over time, and connections between modes carry the transshipment cost. County centroids are connected by wagon routes to nearby railroads and waterways, and directly to every other centroid within 300 kilometers. Finally, because a centroid's distance to a railroad misstates the average distance within the county, the wagon connection is set to the mean distance to the nearest railroad (or river, or canal) from 200 random points in the county, which captures the intensive margin of access as the network becomes denser.

Lowest-cost routes between all pairs of counties, about 5 million calculations per scenario, are found with Dijkstra's algorithm for the 1870 and 1890 networks and for each counterfactual network. The dollar cost per ton is converted into the proportional cost τod\tau_{od}τod​ with Fogel's average value of transported agricultural goods. The main limitations are that the network is essentially domestic, that freight rates are national averages held fixed between 1870 and 1890 (so measured changes come only from the network), that rates do not vary by direction, and that there is no congestion, no economies of scale, no difference in gauges and no role for speed beyond the storage adjustment in the waterway rate.

Empirical Specification

The main specification regresses the log value of agricultural land in county ooo and year ttt on log market access:

ln⁡Vot=βln⁡(MAot)+δo+δst+f(xo,yo)δt+ϵot(23)\ln V_{ot}=\beta\ln\left(MA_{ot}\right)+\delta_o+\delta_{st}+f(x_o,y_o)\delta_t+\epsilon_{ot} \tag{23}lnVot​=βln(MAot​)+δo​+δst​+f(xo​,yo​)δt​+ϵot​(23)

where δo\delta_oδo​ is a county fixed effect, δst\delta_{st}δst​ are state-by-year fixed effects, and f(xo,yo)δtf(x_o,y_o)\delta_tf(xo​,yo​)δt​ is a cubic polynomial in county latitude and longitude interacted with year effects. With the two years 1870 and 1890 the equation is estimated in differences, so that changes in log land value are related to changes in log market access within states and conditional on location. The model interprets β\betaβ as (1+γ)/(1+αθ)(1+\gamma)/(1+\alpha\theta)(1+γ)/(1+αθ) and the controls as absorbing the productivity term. Regressions are weighted by 1870 land value, which limits the influence of outliers and gives the average effect relevant for the counterfactual, and standard errors are clustered by state. The sample is a balanced panel of 2,327 counties; market access is computed over all counties with population data. Changes in market access are large: the residual standard deviation of the log change, net of state fixed effects and location controls, is 0.20 weighted and 0.54 unweighted.

Estimated Impact of Market Access

  • Baseline: β=0.511\beta=0.511β=0.511 with standard error 0.065. The effect splits about equally between the intensive margin (0.245 on value per farm acre) and the extensive margin (0.266 on farm acres per county acre).

  • Alternative measures: model-derived market access gives 0.587 (0.073), close to the value implied by the structural formula; holding population at 1870 levels gives 0.510 (0.065), so the variation comes from the network and not from population growth; market access to counties beyond 100 miles gives 0.487 (0.064); the unweighted estimate is 0.506 (0.124).

  • Local railroads: adding a control for any railroad track in the county gives 0.434 (0.064); adding a cubic in track mileage, 0.431 (0.082); adding the same controls within 10 miles, 0.343 (0.080); and within 20, 30 and 40 miles, 0.276 (0.075). The effect falls, partly through attenuation, but remains substantial when identified from variation that is independent of local construction.

  • Water market access as instrument: counties near navigable waterways depend less on railroads. Log market access in 1870 computed without railroads predicts the change in log market access with a coefficient of −0.096-0.096−0.096 (0.030) and the change in log land value with a coefficient of −0.109-0.109−0.109 (0.024). The two-stage least squares estimate is 1.142 (0.290), larger and much less precise than the baseline; the authors regard a violation of the exclusion restriction as likely and prefer the estimates with controls.

  • By region: 0.587 (0.245) in the Plains, 0.519 (0.076) in the Midwest, 0.546 (0.125) in the South, 0.476 (0.153) in the Far West and 0.306 (0.063) in the Northeast.

  • Other checks: the Online Appendix reports robustness to alternative values of θ\thetaθ inside and outside the Eaton-Kortum range (including θ=1\theta=1θ=1), to lower waterway costs, higher railroad costs and lower wagon costs, to measuring market size by wealth or by population adjusted for ports and Census undercounting, to access to urban areas or to New York City only, and to rural subsamples and additional regional controls. Because a change in the definition of market access changes β\betaβ mechanically, the relevant test is the stability of the counterfactual loss, which the paper reports to be similar across these variants.

Counterfactual without Railroads

The baseline counterfactual recomputes lowest-cost routes without any railroad, recomputes the approximated market access with populations fixed at 1890 levels, and applies the estimated elasticity. Writing MAoCMA_o^{C}MAoC​ for counterfactual market access (a notation introduced here; the paper describes the calculation in words), the proportional loss of total land value is:

∑oVo,1890[1−(MAoC/MAo,1890)β]∑oVo,1890(24)\frac{\sum_oV_{o,1890}\left[1-\left(MA_o^{C}/MA_{o,1890}\right)^{\beta}\right]}{\sum_oV_{o,1890}} \tag{24}∑o​Vo,1890​∑o​Vo,1890​[1−(MAoC​/MAo,1890​)β]​(24)

The sum covers 2,782 counties, including 455 without land value data in 1870, which account for 8 percent of the loss. Market access falls by 80 percent on average, with a standard deviation of 15 percent and 5th and 95th percentiles of 55 and 99.6 percent. This is within the range of the variation used for estimation: going back from 1890 to 1870 lowers market access by 60 percent on average. A local polynomial fit of residual changes shows that the relationship is close to log-linear.

  • Land value: total agricultural land value falls by 60.2 percent (standard error 4.2), or 4.9 billion dollars of 1890.

  • Annual loss: at the mortgage rate of 7.91 percent this is 386 million dollars (27 million) per year, or 3.22 percent (0.22) of GNP, against Fogel's 2.7 percent and a maximum of 5.35 percent if all land value were lost. With state-level mortgage rates the figures are 3.01 and 4.92 percent.

  • Regions: the loss is 2.5 billion dollars in the Midwest, 0.9 billion in the Plains and 0.5 billion in each of the Northeast, the South and the Far West.

Population Reallocation and Worker Utility

The baseline holds the distribution of population fixed and holds Uˉ\bar{U}Uˉ fixed. The first assumption is relaxed in two ways. Assigning counties their shares of national population in 1870, 1850 or 1830, with the national total at its 1890 level, gives losses of 59.1, 59.3 and 60.1 percent. Alternatively, the model is solved for the counterfactual distribution of population. County productivities AoA_oAo​ for 1890 are backed out from 1890 population shares and trade costs, using θ=8.22\theta=8.22θ=8.22, α=0.19\alpha=0.19α=0.19 and γ=0.60\gamma=0.60γ=0.60; holding them fixed, the equilibrium is recomputed with the trade costs of the network without railroads and with total population NNN unchanged. Inserting the new populations into the approximated market access gives a loss of 56.6 percent. Population shifts from interior regions far from navigable waterways toward interior regions close to them, but large cities remain large and market access depends mainly on access to them, so land values are insensitive to the reallocation. The details of this procedure are in the Online Appendix.

Fixed Uˉ\bar{U}Uˉ and fixed NNN are mutually inconsistent, so the full general equilibrium is solved in two extreme scenarios, now with model-derived market access. The absolute level of market access is indeterminate without a numeraire; the paper uses the population-weighted average of county price indices. With that choice, Cobb-Douglas shares tie aggregate land income to the aggregate wage bill:

∑oqoLo=αγ∑owoNo=αγUˉN∑oNoNPo=αγUˉN(25)\sum_oq_oL_o=\frac{\alpha}{\gamma}\sum_ow_oN_o=\frac{\alpha}{\gamma}\bar{U}N\sum_o\frac{N_o}{N}P_o=\frac{\alpha}{\gamma}\bar{U}N \tag{25}o∑​qo​Lo​=γα​o∑​wo​No​=γα​UˉNo∑​NNo​​Po​=γα​UˉN(25)

The paper states the implication in words: the proportional fall in total land value equals the proportional fall in NNN when Uˉ\bar{U}Uˉ is fixed, and the proportional fall in Uˉ\bar{U}Uˉ when NNN is fixed.

  • Fixed utility, elastic migration: land value falls by 58.4 percent and total United States population falls by the same 58.4 percent. Land is the only fixed factor and bears the entire loss, and in a multisector economy part of the adjustment would occur across sectors.

  • Fixed population, endogenous utility: land value falls by 19.0 percent and worker utility falls by 19 percent. Much of the incidence shifts from land to labor, so the aggregate loss is a far larger share of the economy than the land value loss.

  • Which is closer: regressing log population on log market access in the main specification gives 0.259 (0.049), or 0.314 (0.056) with model-derived market access, about one third of the 0.75 implied by perfect mobility. With intermediate mobility, removing railroads would plausibly lower both total population and worker utility.

Alternative Transportation Responses

Each scenario replaces the 1890 network, recomputes market access with fixed population and applies β\betaβ.

  • Extended canals: replacing railroads with Fogel's proposed canals, which bring 70 percent of the infeasible region within 40 miles of a waterway, leaves a loss of 52.4 percent (4.2). The canals mitigate 13 percent of the loss, against 30 percent in Fogel's calculation. Their annual gain of 50 million dollars exceeds their annual capital cost of 34 million dollars without railroads, but is only 0.20 million dollars when railroads exist.

  • Improved country roads: lowering the wagon rate from 23.1 to 14 cents per straight-line ton-mile (from 16.5 to 10 cents per mile traveled) leaves a loss of 47.5 percent (3.9), a mitigation of 21 percent. The annual benefit of the lower wagon rate is 81 million dollars without railroads and 50 million dollars with them, so railroads did not much reduce the incentive to improve roads.

  • Canals and roads together: the loss is 40.0 percent (3.7), a mitigation of 33.6 percent against 34.1 percent for the sum of the two, so the measures are not complementary.

  • Cheaper wagons: at 5, 2.5 and 1 cents per mile traveled, land value falls by 30.6 percent (3.0), falls by 15.2 percent (1.7) and rises by 7.5 percent (1.1); only a wagon rate close to the railroad rate compensates for the absence of railroads.

  • Higher water rates: if the absence of railroad competition doubled waterway rates (Holmes and Schmitz 2001), the loss is 72.5 percent (4.2), 20 percent above the baseline.

The broader lesson is methodological. When treatment spillovers operate at national scale, theory can define a treatment intensity that includes direct and indirect effects, after which relative comparisons across units identify an aggregate effect. The estimates cover only agriculture and static gains from trade, and leave out manufacturing, passenger travel and technological change.

This is the definition of the ideal (exact) price index that belongs to CES preferences: PoP_oPo​ is the minimum expenditure needed to buy one unit of the CES aggregate in county ooo, as the derivation of equation (1) shows (Yo=UPoY_o=UP_oYo​=UPo​). The condition follows from the indirect utility of equation (1) and free mobility. A worker living in county ooo supplies one unit of labor and earns the wage wow_owo​, so by equation (1) the worker's utility is

Compared with the constant printed in the paper's note, the first and last terms agree. The second term is −ln⁡(α/γ)-\ln(\alpha/\gamma)−ln(α/γ), a ratio of the land and labor shares, where the paper prints the trade elasticity in the denominator; and the term −1θln⁡ρ-\frac{1}{\theta}\ln\rho−θ1​lnρ, which arises because the wage depends on consumer market access MAo/ρMA_o/\rhoMAo​/ρ, is missing in the paper. This is the bridge between the model's variable, the annual rental rate of land qoq_oqo​, and the Census variable, the value of agricultural land VoV_oVo​. It is the price of a perpetuity: an asset that pays qoq_oqo​ per year forever, discounted at a constant interest rate rrr, is worth

Vo=∑s=1∞qo(1+r)s=qorV_o=\sum_{s=1}^{\infty}\frac{q_o}{(1+r)^s}=\frac{q_o}{r}Vo​=s=1∑∞​(1+r)sqo​​=rqo​​

The assumption behind it is that current rents are expected to persist (no anticipated growth in rents) and that the discount rate is constant. In logs, ln⁡Vo=ln⁡qo−ln⁡r\ln V_o=\ln q_o-\ln rlnVo​=lnqo​−lnr, so the rent equation (15) holds for land value with the constant shifted by −ln⁡r-\ln r−lnr, and the elasticity with respect to market access is unchanged. This is why the note says the results are unaffected if the interest rate varies by county, by state and year, or with the controls: those components of ln⁡r\ln rlnr are absorbed by the county fixed effects, the state-by-year fixed effects and the location controls of equation (23). What would bias the estimate is a change in expected rent growth or in local interest rates that is correlated with the change in market access within states, for example if land buyers in 1870 already priced in railroads to be built later, which would attenuate the estimate.

The same relation is used in reverse in the counterfactuals: a loss of land value is converted into an annual flow by multiplying by the mortgage rate of 7.91 percent, so a loss of 4.9 billion dollars of land value is 386 million dollars per year. The symbol rrr here is an interest rate; in equations (3) and (7) the same letter denotes the rental rate of capital, as in the paper.

This is the empirical measure of market access used in almost all regressions. It replaces the exact system of equation (14),

MAo=κ3∑dτod−θMAd−(1+θ)θNdMA_o=\kappa_3\sum_d\tau_{od}^{-\theta}MA_d^{\frac{-(1+\theta)}{\theta}}N_dMAo​=κ3​d∑​τod−θ​MAdθ−(1+θ)​​Nd​

by a sum in which the term MAd−(1+θ)/θMA_d^{-(1+\theta)/\theta}MAd−(1+θ)/θ​ of every destination is treated as a common constant, and drops the scale κ3\kappa_3κ3​. The approximation is exact up to scale if all destinations have the same market access, and it is good when the variation in ln⁡MAd\ln MA_dlnMAd​ across the destinations that matter for county ooo is small relative to the variation in τod−θNd\tau_{od}^{-\theta}N_dτod−θ​Nd​. The scale is irrelevant because the regression is in logs with fixed effects.

Each term has a simple reading: NdN_dNd​ is the size of destination ddd (population in place of unobserved income), and τod−θ\tau_{od}^{-\theta}τod−θ​ discounts it by the trade cost with the trade elasticity as exponent, so distant or badly connected markets count for little. The measure needs only populations, the trade-cost matrix from the network database and a value of θ\thetaθ. It does not require solving the model, which makes it less dependent on the model's structure; the cost is that it ignores the competition effect, namely that a destination which is itself well connected is a tougher market. In practice the paper excludes the county's own population, using ∑d≠oτod−θNd\sum_{d\neq o}\tau_{od}^{-\theta}N_d∑d=o​τod−θ​Nd​, to limit the mechanical correlation between a county's land value and its own population, and it checks robustness with populations held at 1870 levels and with the model-derived measure. The coefficient is 0.511 with the approximation and 0.587 with the model-derived term. The counterfactual of equation (24) recomputes this sum with trade costs from a network without railroads.

This expression is the market potential of Harris (1954), written in the notation of the note for comparison with the approximated market access of equation (20). It sums the sizes NdN_dNd​ of all other markets, each divided by the cost of reaching it. Harris used distance as the cost measure, so his index is a population-weighted sum of inverse distances.

Two differences from equation (20) matter. First, the cost measure: with distance, the index of a county changes over time only through population changes elsewhere, because distances are fixed; with the freight cost τod\tau_{od}τod​ computed on the transport network, the index changes when railroads are built, which is the variation the paper uses. Second, the exponent: Harris's index has exponent −1-1−1, equation (20) has −θ-\theta−θ with a value near 8. A larger exponent makes market access much more local. For example, a market whose trade cost is 10 percent higher receives a weight lower by

1−1.1−1≈0.09versus1−1.1−8.22≈0.541-1.1^{-1}\approx0.09\qquad\text{versus}\qquad 1-1.1^{-8.22}\approx0.541−1.1−1≈0.09versus1−1.1−8.22≈0.54

under the two exponents. The model therefore gives a foundation for a market-potential regressor and also disciplines the distance decay through the trade elasticity. The paper reports in its Online Appendix that results are robust to other values of the exponent, including 1; since the regression coefficient changes mechanically with the exponent, the comparison is made on the counterfactual loss and not on the coefficient. The equation is not used in estimation; it serves only to relate the measure to the earlier literature.

This is the nonlinear least squares problem that estimates the trade elasticity. It is the rent equation (15) written for county ooo in year ttt and split into a part that depends on the data through θ\thetaθ and a residual. The regression function f(θ)otf(\theta)_{ot}f(θ)ot​ is the structural elasticity times the log of the model-derived market access MA(θ)otMA(\theta)_{ot}MA(θ)ot​, the solution of the system in equation (14) for the given θ\thetaθ, the trade costs τodt\tau_{odt}τodt​ and the populations NotN_{ot}Not​. The residual εot\varepsilon_{ot}εot​ is the unobserved productivity per unit of land, scaled by 1/(1+αθ)1/(1+\alpha\theta)1/(1+αθ). The constant κ4\kappa_4κ4​, the interest rate that converts rents into values (equation (19)) and the fixed part of productivity are not written; they are handled by the fixed effects and controls of equation (23), conditional on which the estimation is carried out.

The parameter θ\thetaθ enters in two places: in the slope,

1+γ1+αθ\frac{1+\gamma}{1+\alpha\theta}1+αθ1+γ​

and inside the regressor, through the exponent on trade costs and the fixed point of equation (14). With the factor shares fixed at 0.19 and 0.60 there is a single unknown. The estimator chooses the θ\thetaθ that minimizes the sum of squared residuals over a grid of 1,000 values. Identification comes from how fast land values respond to market access changes of different spatial reach: a high θ\thetaθ implies a small slope and a market access measure dominated by nearby markets, a low θ\thetaθ the opposite. The identifying assumption is that changes in productivity are uncorrelated with changes in market access conditional on the controls. The estimate is 8.22, with a wide 95 percent confidence interval from 3.73 to 26.83, which implies a slope of about 0.62, close to the 0.587 estimated freely with the model-derived measure.

This is the main estimating equation, the empirical counterpart of the rent equation (15). The outcome ln⁡Vot\ln V_{ot}lnVot​ is the log of the total value of agricultural land in county ooo in year ttt (1870 or 1890), which by equation (19) equals ln⁡qot\ln q_{ot}lnqot​ minus the log interest rate. The regressor is the log of the approximated market access of equation (20). The county fixed effect δo\delta_oδo​ absorbs time-invariant productivity, land area and location; the state-by-year effects δst\delta_{st}δst​ absorb state-level shocks to productivity, interest rates and prices and the national constant κ4\kappa_4κ4​ (hence the utility level); the term f(xo,yo)δtf(x_o,y_o)\delta_tf(xo​,yo​)δt​, a cubic in latitude and longitude with year-specific coefficients, absorbs smooth spatial trends such as westward expansion. The error ϵot\epsilon_{ot}ϵot​ contains the remaining change in ln⁡(Aot/Lot)\ln(A_{ot}/L_{ot})ln(Aot​/Lot​) scaled by 1/(1+αθ)1/(1+\alpha\theta)1/(1+αθ).

With two periods the equation is equivalent to a regression in differences:

Δln⁡Vo=β Δln⁡MAo+Δδs+f(xo,yo)Δδ+Δϵo\Delta\ln V_o=\beta\,\Delta\ln MA_o+\Delta\delta_s+f(x_o,y_o)\Delta\delta+\Delta\epsilon_oΔlnVo​=βΔlnMAo​+Δδs​+f(xo​,yo​)Δδ+Δϵo​

so β\betaβ is identified from differential changes in market access between 1870 and 1890 among counties in the same state, conditional on location. The model interprets it as

β=1+γ1+αθ\beta=\frac{1+\gamma}{1+\alpha\theta}β=1+αθ1+γ​

The identifying assumption is that changes in county productivity are uncorrelated with changes in market access given the controls. The main threat is that railroads were built toward counties with improving prospects; this motivates the controls for local railroads, the fixed-1870-population measure and the water market access instrument. Because market access depends on the whole network, much of its variation comes from construction far from the county. A value of 0.511 means that a 10 percent rise in market access raises land value by about 5 percent. Regressions are weighted by 1870 land value and standard errors are clustered by state.

The formula applies the estimated specification (23) to a counterfactual change in market access. Write equation (23) for county ooo in 1890 twice, once with actual market access MAo,1890MA_{o,1890}MAo,1890​ and once with counterfactual market access MAoCMA_o^{C}MAoC​ (computed from equation (20) with trade costs of the network without railroads and 1890 populations), holding the fixed effects, the controls and the error term fixed. Subtracting,

ln⁡VoC−ln⁡Vo,1890=β[ln⁡MAoC−ln⁡MAo,1890]⟹VoC=Vo,1890(MAoCMAo,1890)β\ln V_o^{C}-\ln V_{o,1890}=\beta\left[\ln MA_o^{C}-\ln MA_{o,1890}\right]\quad\Longrightarrow\quad V_o^{C}=V_{o,1890}\left(\frac{MA_o^{C}}{MA_{o,1890}}\right)^{\beta}lnVoC​−lnVo,1890​=β[lnMAoC​−lnMAo,1890​]⟹VoC​=Vo,1890​(MAo,1890​MAoC​​)β

where VoCV_o^{C}VoC​ denotes the counterfactual land value. The loss in county ooo in dollars is

Vo,1890−VoC=Vo,1890[1−(MAoCMAo,1890)β]V_{o,1890}-V_o^{C}=V_{o,1890}\left[1-\left(\frac{MA_o^{C}}{MA_{o,1890}}\right)^{\beta}\right]Vo,1890​−VoC​=Vo,1890​[1−(MAo,1890​MAoC​​)β]

Summing over counties and dividing by the total value of land in 1890 gives the proportional loss:

∑o(Vo,1890−VoC)∑oVo,1890=∑oVo,1890[1−(MAoC/MAo,1890)β]∑oVo,1890\frac{\sum_o\left(V_{o,1890}-V_o^{C}\right)}{\sum_oV_{o,1890}}=\frac{\sum_oV_{o,1890}\left[1-\left(MA_o^{C}/MA_{o,1890}\right)^{\beta}\right]}{\sum_oV_{o,1890}}∑o​Vo,1890​∑o​(Vo,1890​−VoC​)​=∑o​Vo,1890​∑o​Vo,1890​[1−(MAoC​/MAo,1890​)β]​

The aggregate loss is a land-value-weighted average of county losses, which is why the regression is weighted by land value. As a check on magnitudes, a county whose market access falls by 80 percent keeps the fraction 0.20.511≈0.440.2^{0.511}\approx0.440.20.511≈0.44 of its land value, a loss of 56 percent, near the reported aggregate of 60.2 percent. The formula is the note's notation for a calculation the paper describes in words, and it is correct under the assumptions stated: log-linearity over a large change, unchanged productivity, fixed utility level (the constant κ4\kappa_4κ4​) and fixed populations. Holding the state-by-year effects fixed means that the comparison across counties within a state is extrapolated to the level, the step that the general equilibrium exercises of equation (25) examine.

The identity links aggregate land income to aggregate population and worker utility. From the derivation of equation (3), in every county land earns the share α\alphaα and labor the share γ\gammaγ of income:

qoLo=αYo,woNo=γYo⟹qoLo=αγwoNoq_oL_o=\alpha Y_o,\qquad w_oN_o=\gamma Y_o\quad\Longrightarrow\quad q_oL_o=\frac{\alpha}{\gamma}w_oN_oqo​Lo​=αYo​,wo​No​=γYo​⟹qo​Lo​=γα​wo​No​

Sum over counties and replace the wage by the free-mobility condition of equation (5), wo=UˉPow_o=\bar{U}P_owo​=UˉPo​:

∑oqoLo=αγ∑owoNo=αγUˉ∑oNoPo=αγUˉN∑oNoNPo\sum_oq_oL_o=\frac{\alpha}{\gamma}\sum_ow_oN_o=\frac{\alpha}{\gamma}\bar{U}\sum_oN_oP_o=\frac{\alpha}{\gamma}\bar{U}N\sum_o\frac{N_o}{N}P_oo∑​qo​Lo​=γα​o∑​wo​No​=γα​Uˉo∑​No​Po​=γα​UˉNo∑​NNo​​Po​

The last step multiplies and divides by total population N=∑oNoN=\sum_oN_oN=∑o​No​. The remaining sum is the population-weighted average of county price indices, which the paper chooses as numeraire and so sets to one in every equilibrium:

∑oNoNPo=1⟹∑oqoLo=αγUˉN\sum_o\frac{N_o}{N}P_o=1\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\sum_oq_oL_o=\frac{\alpha}{\gamma}\bar{U}No∑​NNo​​Po​=1⟹o∑​qo​Lo​=γα​UˉN

The identity is not printed in the paper, but it is what lies behind the paper's statement that Cobb-Douglas production and the choice of numeraire tie the fall in land value to the fall in population or utility. Compare the equilibrium with railroads to the one without, marked by a prime:

∑oqo′Lo∑oqoLo=Uˉ′N′UˉN\frac{\sum_oq_o'L_o}{\sum_oq_oL_o}=\frac{\bar{U}'N'}{\bar{U}N}∑o​qo​Lo​∑o​qo′​Lo​​=UˉNUˉ′N′​

With utility fixed the proportional fall in aggregate land rent equals the proportional fall in NNN (58.4 percent for both); with population fixed it equals the proportional fall in Uˉ\bar{U}Uˉ (19.0 percent for both). With land value proportional to rent at a fixed interest rate (equation (19)), the same holds for total land value. The identity is exact given the numeraire; under another numeraire, such as the price index of New York City, the ratio also contains the change in the population-weighted average price index and the two percentages need not coincide exactly.
